I think my advise would vary a bit depending on the person, their setup, and their needs. For myself, as an example, what worked best was rather than using a VM or a dual-boot configuration, i just took an older computer, threw on a linux distro and just had two computers at my desk. This was already a very effective setup for me when I used two (or more) Windows boxes and it meant that: (1) there was no delay for rebooting or bringing up a VM and (2) if something went wrong or that I didn't understand (which was inevitable for a new user), I could research the issue on the other computer without impacting the state of the linux box in question.

Now, that said, that's not a solution that would work for everyone (obviously). I think for most people, I would probably advocate a hybrid solution: start with some VMs. They're easy to setup (and discard), so you can quickly/easily try multiple distros - even multiple distros at the same time. Take a few months and settle in to one you like. Then look at how to get it to dual-boot. Dual-booting will get you the best possible system performance, but is a more intensive operation (as compared to setting up a VM or using a second box). Make sure....seriously... that you have everything you need from your Windows partition backed up and that you have a real plan for backing out. Messing with the boot loader is never something to take lightly.

Ultimately, your core plan - a slow transition is a good one and certainly one that I would support. Just make sure that, however you do the technology part, that you're taking advantage of the linux install as often as possible and for as many things as possible, as soon as you're able to. This is how you will get comfortable with linux, and slowly-but-surely it will become your main OS and the Windows instance will be the one in the VM/other-partition/lesser-box. :)
